L107: # The Go Programming Language Specification
L108: 
L109: ## Language version go1.27 (May 26, 2026)
L110: ## Introduction
L111: 
L112: This is the reference manual for the Go programming language. For more information and other documents, see 【18†go.dev】.
L113: 
L114: Go is a general-purpose language designed with systems programming in mind. It is strongly typed and garbage-collected and has explicit support for concurrent programming. Programs are constructed from packages, whose properties allow efficient management of dependencies.
L115: The syntax is compact and simple to parse, allowing for easy analysis by automatic tools such as integrated development environments.
L116: ## Notation
L117: 
L118: The syntax is specified using a 【19†variant†en.wikipedia.org】 of Extended Backus-Naur Form (EBNF):
L119: 
L120:     Syntax      = { Production } .
L121:     Production  = production_name "=" [ Expression ] "." .
L122:     Expression  = Term { "|" Term } .
L123:     Term        = Factor { Factor } .
L124:     Factor      = production_name | token [ "…" token ] | Group | Option | Repetition .
L125:     Group       = "(" Expression ")" .
L126:     Option      = "[" Expression "]" .
L127:     Repetition  = "{" Expression "}" .
L128: Productions are expressions constructed from terms and the following operators, in increasing precedence:
L129: 
L130:     |   alternation
L131:     ()  grouping
L132:     []  option (0 or 1 times)
L133:     {}  repetition (0 to n times)
L134: 
L135: 
L136: Lowercase production names are used to identify lexical (terminal) tokens. Non-terminals are in CamelCase. Lexical tokens are enclosed in double quotes `""` or back quotes ````.
L137: The form `a … b` represents the set of characters from `a` through `b` as alternatives. The horizontal ellipsis `…` is also used elsewhere in the spec to informally denote various enumerations or code snippets that are not further specified. The character `…` (as opposed to the three characters `...`) is not a token of the Go language.
L138: A link of the form [【20†Go 1.xx】] indicates that a described language feature (or some aspect of it) was changed or added with language version 1.xx and thus requires at minimum that language version to build. For details, see the 【20†linked section】 in the 【21†appendix】.
L139: ## Source code representation
L140: 
L141: Source code is Unicode text encoded in 【22†UTF-8†en.wikipedia.org】. The text is not canonicalized, so a single accented code point is distinct from the same character constructed from combining an accent and a letter; those are treated as two code points. For simplicity, this document will use the unqualified term character to refer to a Unicode code point in the source text.
L142: Each code point is distinct; for instance, uppercase and lowercase letters are different characters.
L143: 
L144: Implementation restriction: For compatibility with other tools, a compiler may disallow the NUL character (U+0000) in the source text.
L145: 
L146: Implementation restriction: For compatibility with other tools, a compiler may ignore a UTF-8-encoded byte order mark (U+FEFF) if it is the first Unicode code point in the source text. A byte order mark may be disallowed anywhere else in the source.
L147: ### Characters
L148: 
L149: The following terms are used to denote specific Unicode character categories:
L150: 
L151:     newline        = /* the Unicode code point U+000A */ .
L152:     unicode_char   = /* an arbitrary Unicode code point except newline */ .
L153:     unicode_letter = /* a Unicode code point categorized as "Letter" */ .
L154:     unicode_digit  = /* a Unicode code point categorized as "Number, decimal digit" */ .
L155: In 【23†The Unicode Standard 8.0†www.unicode.org】, Section 4.5 "General Category" defines a set of character categories. Go treats all characters in any of the Letter categories Lu, Ll, Lt, Lm, or Lo as Unicode letters, and those in the Number category Nd as Unicode digits.
L156: ### Letters and digits
L157: 
L158: The underscore character `_` (U+005F) is considered a lowercase letter.
L159: 
L160:     letter        = 【24†unicode_letter】 | "_" .
L161:     decimal_digit = "0" … "9" .
L162:     binary_digit  = "0" | "1" .
L163:     octal_digit   = "0" … "7" .
L164:     hex_digit     = "0" … "9" | "A" … "F" | "a" … "f" .
L165: 
L166: 
L167: ## Lexical elements
L168: ### Comments
L169: 
L170: Comments serve as program documentation. There are two forms:
L171: 
L172:   1. Line comments start with the character sequence `//` and stop at the end of the line.
L173:   2. General comments start with the character sequence `/*` and stop with the first subsequent character sequence `*/`.
L174: 
L175: A comment cannot start inside a 【25†rune】 or 【26†string literal】, or inside a comment. A general comment containing no newlines acts like a space. Any other comment acts like a newline.
L176: ### Tokens
L177: Tokens form the vocabulary of the Go language. There are four classes: identifiers, keywords, operators and punctuation, and literals. White space, formed from spaces (U+0020), horizontal tabs (U+0009), carriage returns (U+000D), and newlines (U+000A), is ignored except as it separates tokens that would otherwise combine into a single token. Also, a newline or end of file may trigger the insertion of a 【27†semicolon】.
L178: While breaking the input into tokens, the next token is the longest sequence of characters that form a valid token.
L179: ### Semicolons
L180: 
L181: The formal syntax uses semicolons `";"` as terminators in a number of productions. Go programs may omit most of these semicolons using the following two rules:
L182:   1. When the input is broken into tokens, a semicolon is automatically inserted into the token stream immediately after a line's final token if that token is
L183:      * an 【28†identifier】
L184:      * an 【29†integer】, 【30†floating-point】, 【31†imaginary】, 【25†rune】, or 【26†string】 literal
L185:      * one of the 【32†keywords】 `break`, `continue`, `fallthrough`, or `return`
L186:      * one of the 【33†operators and punctuation】 `++`, `--`, `)`, `]`, or `}`
L187:   2. To allow complex statements to occupy a single line, a semicolon may be omitted before a closing `")"` or `"}"`.
L188: To reflect idiomatic use, code examples in this document elide semicolons using these rules.
L189: ### Identifiers
L190: 
L191: Identifiers name program entities such as variables and types. An identifier is a sequence of one or more letters and digits. The first character in an identifier must be a letter.
L192: 
L193:     identifier = 【34†letter】 { 【34†letter】 | 【35†unicode_digit】 } .
L194: 
L195: 
L196:     a
L197:     _x9
L198:     ThisVariableIsExported
L199:     αβ
L200: 
L201: 
L202: Some identifiers are 【36†predeclared】.
L203: ### Keywords
L204: 
L205: The following keywords are reserved and may not be used as identifiers.
L206: 
L207:     break        default      func         interface    select
L208:     case         defer        go           map          struct
L209:     chan         else         goto         package      switch
L210:     const        fallthrough  if           range        type
L211:     continue     for          import       return       var
L212: ### Operators and punctuation
L213: 
L214: The following character sequences represent 【37†operators】 (including 【38†assignment operators】) and punctuation [【39†Go 1.18】]:
L215: 
L216:     +    &     +=    &=     &&    ==    !=    (    )
L217:     -    |     -=    |=     ||    <     <=    [    ]
L218:     *    ^     *=    ^=     <-    >     >=    {    }
L219:     /    <<    /=    <<=    ++    =     :=    ,    ;
L220:     %    >>    %=    >>=    --    !     ...   .    :
L221:          &^          &^=          ~
L222: ### Integer literals
L223: 
L224: An integer literal is a sequence of digits representing an 【40†integer constant】. An optional prefix sets a non-decimal base: `0b` or `0B` for binary, `0`, `0o`, or `0O` for octal, and `0x` or `0X` for hexadecimal [【41†Go 1.13】]. A single `0` is considered a decimal zero. In hexadecimal literals, letters `a` through `f` and `A` through `F` represent values 10 through 15.
L225: For readability, an underscore character `_` may appear after a base prefix or between successive digits; such underscores do not change the literal's value.
L226: 
L227:     int_lit        = 【42†decimal_lit】 | 【43†binary_lit】 | 【44†octal_lit】 | 【45†hex_lit】 .
L228:     decimal_lit    = "0" | ( "1" … "9" ) [ [ "_" ] 【46†decimal_digits】 ] .
L229:     binary_lit     = "0" ( "b" | "B" ) [ "_" ] 【47†binary_digits】 .
L230:     octal_lit      = "0" [ "o" | "O" ] [ "_" ] 【48†octal_digits】 .
L231:     hex_lit        = "0" ( "x" | "X" ) [ "_" ] 【49†hex_digits】 .
L232: 
L233:     decimal_digits = 【50†decimal_digit】 { [ "_" ] 【50†decimal_digit】 } .
L234:     binary_digits  = 【51†binary_digit】 { [ "_" ] 【51†binary_digit】 } .
L235:     octal_digits   = 【52†octal_digit】 { [ "_" ] 【52†octal_digit】 } .
L236:     hex_digits     = 【53†hex_digit】 { [ "_" ] 【53†hex_digit】 } .
L237:

L240:     4_2

L243:     0o600
L244:     0O600       // second character is capital letter 'O'
L245:     0xBadFace

L248:     170141183460469231731687303715884105727

L250: 
L251:     _42         // an identifier, not an integer literal
L252:     42_         // invalid: _ must separate successive digits
L253:     4__2        // invalid: only one _ at a time
L254:     0_xBadFace  // invalid: _ must separate successive digits
L255: ### Floating-point literals
L256: 
L257: A floating-point literal is a decimal or hexadecimal representation of a 【40†floating-point constant】.
L258: A decimal floating-point literal consists of an integer part (decimal digits), a decimal point, a fractional part (decimal digits), and an exponent part (`e` or `E` followed by an optional sign and decimal digits). One of the integer part or the fractional part may be elided; one of the decimal point or the exponent part may be elided. An exponent value exp scales the mantissa (integer and fractional part) by 10^{exp}.
L259: A hexadecimal floating-point literal consists of a `0x` or `0X` prefix, an integer part (hexadecimal digits), a radix point, a fractional part (hexadecimal digits), and an exponent part (`p` or `P` followed by an optional sign and decimal digits). One of the integer part or the fractional part may be elided; the radix point may be elided as well, but the exponent part is required.
L260: (This syntax matches the one given in IEEE 754-2008 §5.12.3.) An exponent value exp scales the mantissa (integer and fractional part) by 2^{exp} [【41†Go 1.13】].
L261: For readability, an underscore character `_` may appear after a base prefix or between successive digits; such underscores do not change the literal value.
L262: 
L263:     float_lit         = 【54†decimal_float_lit】 | 【55†hex_float_lit】 .
L264: 
L265:     decimal_float_lit = 【46†decimal_digits】 "." [ 【46†decimal_digits】 ] [ 【56†decimal_exponent】 ] |
L266:                         【46†decimal_digits】 【56†decimal_exponent】 |
L267:                         "." 【46†decimal_digits】 [ 【56†decimal_exponent】 ] .
L268:     decimal_exponent  = ( "e" | "E" ) [ "+" | "-" ] 【46†decimal_digits】 .
L269: 
L270:     hex_float_lit     = "0" ( "x" | "X" ) 【57†hex_mantissa】 【58†hex_exponent】 .
L271:     hex_mantissa      = [ "_" ] 【49†hex_digits】 "." [ 【49†hex_digits】 ] |
L272:                         [ "_" ] 【49†hex_digits】 |
L273:                         "." 【49†hex_digits】 .
L274:     hex_exponent      = ( "p" | "P" ) [ "+" | "-" ] 【46†decimal_digits】 .

L304: ### Imaginary literals
L305: 
L306: An imaginary literal represents the imaginary part of a 【40†complex constant】. It consists of an 【29†integer】 or 【30†floating-point】 literal followed by the lowercase letter `i`. The value of an imaginary literal is the value of the respective integer or floating-point literal multiplied by the imaginary unit i [【41†Go 1.13】]
L307: 
L308:     imaginary_lit = (【46†decimal_digits】 | 【59†int_lit】 | 【60†float_lit】) "i" .
L309: For backward compatibility, an imaginary literal's integer part consisting entirely of decimal digits (and possibly underscores) is considered a decimal integer, even if it starts with a leading `0`.
L310: 
L311:     0i
L312:     0123i         // == 123i for backward-compatibility
L313:     0o123i        // == 0o123 * 1i == 83i
L314:     0xabci        // == 0xabc * 1i == 2748i
L315:     0.i
L316:     2.71828i
L317:     1.e+0i
L318:     6.67428e-11i
L319:     1E6i
L320:     .25i
L321:     .12345E+5i
L322:     0x1p-2i       // == 0x1p-2 * 1i == 0.25i
L323: ### Rune literals
L324: 
L325: A rune literal represents a 【40†rune constant】, an integer value identifying a Unicode code point. A rune literal is expressed as one or more characters enclosed in single quotes, as in `'x'` or `'\n'`. Within the quotes, any character may appear except newline and unescaped single quote. A single quoted character represents the Unicode value of the character itself, while multi-character sequences beginning with a backslash encode values in various formats.
L326: The simplest form represents the single character within the quotes; since Go source text is Unicode characters encoded in UTF-8, multiple UTF-8-encoded bytes may represent a single integer value. For instance, the literal `'a'` holds a single byte representing a literal `a`, Unicode U+0061, value `0x61`, while `'ä'` holds two bytes (`0xc3` `0xa4`) representing a literal `a`-dieresis, U+00E4, value `0xe4`.
L327: Several backslash escapes allow arbitrary values to be encoded as ASCII text. There are four ways to represent the integer value as a numeric constant: `\x` followed by exactly two hexadecimal digits; `\u` followed by exactly four hexadecimal digits; `\U` followed by exactly eight hexadecimal digits, and a plain backslash `\` followed by exactly three octal digits. In each case the value of the literal is the value represented by the digits in the corresponding base.
L328: Although these representations all result in an integer, they have different valid ranges. Octal escapes must represent a value between 0 and 255 inclusive. Hexadecimal escapes satisfy this condition by construction. The escapes `\u` and `\U` represent Unicode code points so within them some values are illegal, in particular those above `0x10FFFF` and surrogate halves.
L329: After a backslash, certain single-character escapes represent special values:
L330: 
L331:     \a   U+0007 alert or bell
L332:     \b   U+0008 backspace
L333:     \f   U+000C form feed
L334:     \n   U+000A line feed or newline
L335:     \r   U+000D carriage return
L336:     \t   U+0009 horizontal tab
L337:     \v   U+000B vertical tab
L338:     \\   U+005C backslash
L339:     \'   U+0027 single quote  (valid escape only within rune literals)
L340:     \"   U+0022 double quote  (valid escape only within string literals)
L341: An unrecognized character following a backslash in a rune literal is illegal.
L342: 
L343:     rune_lit         = "'" ( 【61†unicode_value】 | 【62†byte_value】 ) "'" .
L344:     unicode_value    = 【63†unicode_char】 | 【64†little_u_value】 | 【65†big_u_value】 | 【66†escaped_char】 .
L345:     byte_value       = 【67†octal_byte_value】 | 【68†hex_byte_value】 .
L346:     octal_byte_value = `\` 【52†octal_digit】 【52†octal_digit】 【52†octal_digit】 .

L350:                                【53†hex_digit】 【53†hex_digit】 【53†hex_digit】 【53†hex_digit】 .

L373: ### String literals
L374: 
L375: A string literal represents a 【40†string constant】 obtained from concatenating a sequence of characters. There are two forms: raw string literals and interpreted string literals.
L376: Raw string literals are character sequences between back quotes, as in ``foo``. Within the quotes, any character may appear except back quote. The value of a raw string literal is the string composed of the uninterpreted (implicitly UTF-8-encoded) characters between the quotes; in particular, backslashes have no special meaning and the string may contain newlines. Carriage return characters ('\r') inside raw string literals are discarded from the raw string value.
L377: Interpreted string literals are character sequences between double quotes, as in `"bar"`. Within the quotes, any character may appear except newline and unescaped double quote. The text between the quotes forms the value of the literal, with backslash escapes interpreted as they are in 【25†rune literals】 (except that `\'` is illegal and `\"` is legal), with the same restrictions.
L378: The three-digit octal (`\`nnn) and two-digit hexadecimal (`\x`nn) escapes represent individual bytes of the resulting string; all other escapes represent the (possibly multi-byte) UTF-8 encoding of individual characters. Thus inside a string literal `\377` and `\xFF` represent a single byte of value `0xFF`=255, while `ÿ`, `\u00FF`, `\U000000FF` and `\xc3\xbf` represent the two bytes `0xc3` `0xbf` of the UTF-8 encoding of character U+00FF.
L379: 
L380:     string_lit             = 【69†raw_string_lit】 | 【70†interpreted_string_lit】 .
L381:     raw_string_lit         = "`" { 【63†unicode_char】 | 【71†newline】 } "`" .
L382:     interpreted_string_lit = `"` { 【61†unicode_value】 | 【62†byte_value】 } `"` .
L383: 
L384: 
L385:     `abc`                // same as "abc"
L386:     `\n
L387:     \n`                  // same as "\\n\n\\n"
L388:     "\n"
L389:     "\""                 // same as `"`
L390:     "Hello, world!\n"
L391:     "日本語"
L392:     "\u65e5本\U00008a9e"
L393:     "\xff\u00FF"
L394:     "\uD800"             // illegal: surrogate half
L395:     "\U00110000"         // illegal: invalid Unicode code point
L396: These examples all represent the same string:
L397: 
L398:     "日本語"                                 // UTF-8 input text
L399:     `日本語`                                 // UTF-8 input text as a raw literal
L400:     "\u65e5\u672c\u8a9e"                    // the explicit Unicode code points
L401:     "\U000065e5\U0000672c\U00008a9e"        // the explicit Unicode code points
L402:     "\xe6\x97\xa5\xe6\x9c\xac\xe8\xaa\x9e"  // the explicit UTF-8 bytes
L403: If the source code represents a character as two code points, such as a combining form involving an accent and a letter, the result will be an error if placed in a rune literal (it is not a single code point), and will appear as two code points if placed in a string literal.
L404: ## Constants
L405: 
L406: There are boolean constants, rune constants, integer constants, floating-point constants, complex constants, and string constants. Rune, integer, floating-point, and complex constants are collectively called numeric constants.
L407: A constant value is represented by a 【25†rune】, 【29†integer】, 【30†floating-point】, 【31†imaginary】, or 【26†string】 literal, an identifier denoting a constant, a 【72†constant expression】, a 【73†conversion】 with a result that is a constant, or the result value of some built-in functions such as `min` or `max` applied to constant arguments, `unsafe.Sizeof` applied to 【74†certain values】, `cap` or `len` applied to 【75†some expressions】, `real` and `imag` applied to a complex constant and `complex` applied to numeric constants.
L408: The boolean truth values are represented by the predeclared constants `true` and `false`. The predeclared identifier 【76†iota】 denotes an integer constant.
L409: In general, complex constants are a form of 【72†constant expression】 and are discussed in that section.
L410: 
L411: Numeric constants represent exact values of arbitrary precision and do not overflow. Consequently, there are no constants denoting the IEEE 754 negative zero, infinity, and not-a-number values.
L412: 
L413: Constants may be 【77†typed】 or untyped. Literal constants, `true`, `false`, `iota`, and certain 【72†constant expressions】 containing only untyped constant operands are untyped.
L414: A constant may be given a type explicitly by a 【78†constant declaration】 or 【73†conversion】, or implicitly when used in a 【79†variable declaration】 or an 【38†assignment statement】 or as an operand in an 【80†expression】. It is an error if the constant value cannot be 【81†represented】 as a value of the respective type. If the type is a type parameter, the constant is converted into a non-constant value of the type parameter.
L415: An untyped constant has a default type which is the type to which the constant is implicitly converted in contexts where a typed value is required, for instance, in a 【82†short variable declaration】 such as `i := 0` where there is no explicit type. The default type of an untyped constant is `bool`, `rune`, `int`, `float64`, `complex128`, or `string` respectively, depending on whether it is a boolean, rune, integer, floating-point, complex, or string constant.
L416: Implementation restriction: Although numeric constants have arbitrary precision in the language, a compiler may implement them using an internal representation with limited precision. That said, every implementation must:
L417:   * Represent integer constants with at least 256 bits.
L418:   * Represent floating-point constants, including the parts of a complex constant, with a mantissa of at least 256 bits and a signed binary exponent of at least 16 bits.
L419:   * Give an error if unable to represent an integer constant precisely.
L420:   * Give an error if unable to represent a floating-point or complex constant due to overflow.
L421:   * Round to the nearest representable constant if unable to represent a floating-point or complex constant due to limits on precision.
L422: These requirements apply both to literal constants and to the result of evaluating 【72†constant expressions】.
L423: ## Variables
L424: 
L425: A variable is a storage location for holding a value. The set of permissible values is determined by the variable's 【77†type】.
L426: A 【79†variable declaration】 or, for function parameters and results, the signature of a 【83†function declaration】 or 【84†function literal】 reserves storage for a named variable. Calling the built-in function 【85†`new`】 or taking the address of a 【86†composite literal】 allocates storage for a variable at run time. Such an anonymous variable is referred to via a (possibly implicit) 【87†pointer indirection】.
L427: Structured variables of 【88†array】, 【89†slice】, and 【90†struct】 types have elements and fields that may be 【87†addressed】 individually. Each such element acts like a variable.
L428: The static type (or just type) of a variable is the type given in its declaration, the type provided in the `new` call or composite literal, or the type of an element of a structured variable. Variables of interface type also have a distinct dynamic type, which is the (non-interface) type of the value assigned to the variable at run time (unless the value is the predeclared identifier `nil`, which has no type).
L429: The dynamic type may vary during execution but values stored in interface variables are always 【91†assignable】 to the static type of the variable.
L430: 
L431:     var x interface{}  // x is nil and has static type interface{}
L432:     var v *T           // v has value nil, static type *T
L433:     x = 42             // x has value 42 and dynamic type int
L434:     x = v              // x has value (*T)(nil) and dynamic type *T
